boilerplate.section_intro: This section consists of questions and problems involving quantitative reasoning.  Each question is followed by four possible responses.  Choose the correct answer and mark its number in the appropriate place on the answer sheet.
boilerplate.section_meta:

The time allotted is 20 minutes.

boilerplate.general_comments_title: General Comments about the Quantitative Reasoning Section
general_comments: The figures accompanying some of the problems are provided to help solve the problems, but are not necessarily drawn to scale.  Therefore, do not rely on the figures alone to deduce line length, angle size, and so forth.
If a line in a figure appears to be straight, you may assume that it is in fact a straight line.
When a geometric term (side, radius, area, volume, etc.) appears in a problem, it refers to a term whose value is greater than 0, unless stated otherwise.
When \(\sqrt{a}\) (a > 0) appears in a problem, it refers to the positive root of a.
"0" is neither a positive nor a negative number.

clusters.intro:
Study the graph below, then answer the five questions that follow.

The graph describes the absences of the eight employees at a certain factory (marked with the letters A-H) during the six months January-June.  Each absence lasted a whole number of weeks.  The absences were classified according to the reason for the absence: course, illness, vacation or business trip (see key).

Note: For the sake of convenience, the number of weeks in each month was rounded, such that some of the months have 4 weeks and some of the months have 5 weeks.

For example, in the third week of March employee C was absent from work because he was on a business trip.

Study the graph below, then answer the four questions that follow.

The graph describes the results of a study that examined the effectiveness of four methods for teaching reading in the first grade (A, B, C and D).

The teaching methods were examined in four first-grade classes, each of which has 30 students.  Each class studied with one of the methods from the beginning of the school year (September 1) until its end (June 30).  At the end of each month the students took a test that examines reading ability.  A student who received a grade of "pass" on the test was considered a student who knows how to read, and was not tested again thereafter.

Each teaching method is marked on the graph by means of a different shape (see key).  The position of the shape relative to the horizontal axis represents the month in the school year, and its position relative to the vertical axis represents the cumulative number of students who received a grade of "pass" from the beginning of the year until the test at the end of this month (inclusive).

Notes:
- All the students who participated in the study did not know how to read at the beginning of the school year.
- The lines connecting the shapes are auxiliary lines only.

For example, in the class that studied with method A there were 6 students at the end of the month of October who know how to read.  Of them, 2 students received a grade of "pass" already on the test administered at the end of the month of September, and were not tested any more thereafter.

questions.stem:
In the accompanying figure, ABCD is a rectangle whose side lengths are 2 cm and 4 cm.
Points E, F, G and H are the midpoints of the sides of the rectangle.

What is the area of the dark quadrilateral (in cm²)?

2% of W is 10.

W = ?

methods.text: 2% is a fiftieth, so the whole is fifty times 10. Reading small percentages as fractions is faster than dividing by a decimal.

questions.stem: On one side of a fair coin the number 1 is written and on its other side the number 0 is written. The coin is tossed three times, and the sum of the numbers obtained is calculated. How many different sums is it possible to obtain?

Hagai travelled on a trip to the USA.  The price of the flight ticket was \(\frac{1}{3}\) of the expenses of the trip.  The price that he paid for renting a car was \(\frac{1}{6}\) of the expenses of the trip.  The rest of the expenses of the trip were 1,500 dollars.

What was the price of the flight ticket?

methods.text: The flight and the car account for \(\frac13 + \frac16 = \frac12\) of the expenses, so the remaining \(\frac12\) is 1,500 dollars and the total is 3,000. The ticket is \(\frac13\) of that: 1,000 dollars.
The fractions are of the same whole, so they add directly — and the leftover being exactly half is what makes the total immediate.

Revital and Beni are preparing a quiche.  Revital peels 8 onions in 7 minutes, and Beni slices 6 onions in 9 minutes.

How many onions will Revital manage to peel in the time that Beni slices 14 onions?

methods.text: Beni slices \(\frac69 = \frac23\) an onion a minute, so 14 onions take 21 minutes.
Revital peels \(\frac87\) a minute, so in 21 minutes she does 24. Find the shared time first, then apply the other rate to it.

questions.stem:
x is any number between 1 and 2  (1 < x < 2).

Which of the following expressions has the greatest value?

methods.text: On \(1<x<2\): \(2x > x^2\) because \(x<2\); \(2x > \frac2x\) because \(x^2>1\); and \(x^x < x^2\) because the exponent is below 2 with a base above 1. So \(2x\) is largest throughout.
Take \(x=1.5\): the four values are 3, 1.33, 2.25 and about 1.84. Testing a second value near 2, say 1.9, keeps \(2x\) ahead at 3.8 against 3.61 and 3.39.

questions.stem: In how many of the months described in the graph was there at least one week in which an employee was absent because he was on a course?

Two employees were each absent for 3 separate periods of absence.

One of the two employees was absent for a total of  ______  weeks more than the other.
Which of the following graphs describes the number of employees who were not absent from work in each of the weeks of the month of June?

Two employees who were never absent from work at the same time are called "coordinated employees".

In the period of time described in the graph, how many of the employees were coordinated with employee H ?

It is known that in the period of time described in the graph only men were absent due to illness. It is also known that in the period of time described in the graph an equal number of men and women went on a course. How many men work at the factory, at the very least?

Given the equation \((x + 1)^2 - (x - 1)^2 = 0\)

How many different values of x satisfy the equation?
options: There is no value of x that satisfies the equation

methods.text: Difference of squares: \((x+1)^2-(x-1)^2 = [2][2x] = 4x\). Setting \(4x = 0\) gives the single value \(x = 0\).
Expanding is just as quick here: the \(x^2\) terms cancel and \(4x\) is left. Either route avoids treating it as a quadratic, which is the trap behind option (2).

questions.stem: x, y and z are numbers that are different from zero. Which of the following expressions is not equal to the expression \(\frac{1}{x} + \frac{1}{y} + \frac{1}{z}\) ?
options: \(\dfrac{x \cdot y + y \cdot z + x \cdot z}{x \cdot y \cdot z}\)

methods.text: Take \(x=1, y=2, z=3\): the original is \(1+\frac12+\frac13 = \frac{11}{6}\). Options (1), (2) and (3) all give \(\frac{11}{6}\); option (4) gives \(\frac{6}{6} = 1\).
Over a common denominator the sum is \(\dfrac{yz+xz+xy}{xyz}\), which is option (1). Option (4) has the letters themselves on top rather than their pairwise products.

questions.stem:
Given: \(a^2 - 2 < a(a + 2)\)

Which of the following statements is necessarily true?
options: None of the above statements is necessarily true

methods.text: Expand the right side: \(a^2-2<a^2+2a\). The \(a^2\) terms cancel, leaving \(-2<2a\), so \(a>-1\). That is all the given says.

Every option compares \(2a\) with \(a\), and that comparison is decided entirely by the sign of \(a\): \(2a>a\) when \(a\) is positive, \(2a<a\) when negative, equal at zero. Since \(a>-1\) permits all three, nothing is necessary.
\(a=1\) satisfies the given and makes \(2a>a\); \(a=-\frac12\) satisfies it too and makes \(2a<a\). Two legal values, two opposite conclusions.

questions.stem: In a sack there are green balls and yellow balls only. The number of green balls is 25% greater than the number of yellow balls. The total number of balls in the sack is necessarily -

methods.text: Let the yellow count be \(y\). Green is \(1.25y = \frac54 y\), so \(y\) must be a multiple of 4 for the count to be whole. The total is \(y + \frac54 y = \frac94 y\).
With \(y = 4k\), the total is \(9k\) — always a multiple of 9. Nothing forces it to be odd, or a multiple of 4 or 25; the 9 comes from the \(\frac94\) and nowhere else.

questions.stem: Daniel had a cylinder of dough whose length is h cm and the radius of its base is \(\pi\) cm. Daniel removed from the cylinder a slice of dough whose volume is \(\pi h\) cm³ and made from the dough that remained a new cylinder whose length is also h cm. What is the radius of the base of the new cylinder (in cm)?

The accompanying figure describes a system of roads composed of ten straight roads.
Every straight segment is a one-way road, and the direction of travel on it is marked in the figure with an arrow.

What is the smallest number of roads that need to be cancelled in order to disconnect A from B (that is, so that it will not be possible to get from A to B)?

Ra'anan set out on a trip of 8 hours.  From the moment that he set out on his way (not including the moment of setting out), every 25 minutes he drank water, and every hour he passed by another hiker.

How many times during the trip did Ra'anan pass by another hiker at the time that he drank water?

methods.text: Both events coincide at common multiples of 25 and 60 minutes. \(\text{LCM}(25,60) = 300\) minutes, which is 5 hours.

Within an 8-hour trip that happens once, at the 5-hour mark — 10 hours would be the next. Note the question excludes the starting moment, which is what makes 0 the wrong answer rather than the right one.

questions.stem: Gilad ran at a constant speed. He ran 32 km in total. The length of time (in hours) in which he ran is equal to half of his speed (in kph). At what speed did Gilad run (in kph)?

methods.text: Time \(= \frac v2\) and distance \(= v \times t\), so \(v \cdot \frac v2 = 32\), giving \(v^2 = 64\) and \(v = 8\).
Four numeric options, one multiplication each: at 8 km/h he runs for 4 hours, and 4 is half of 8 ✓. Faster than solving, and immune to a sign or square-root slip.

methods.text: \(a \neq 0\), so divide both sides by \(a\): \(b - c = 3\), giving \(b = c+3\). The \(a\) disappears entirely.
Options (3) and (4) keep \(a\) in the answer, which cannot be right once \(a\) has been divided out. Two options fall without any algebra.

questions.stem:
Efraim read 5 articles one after the other without breaks.  It is known that every article that Efraim read has a number of pages that is double that in the article that he read before it.  Efraim reads a page in an article in a constant length of time.
Efraim read the first article in \(\frac{1}{2}\) an hour.

Within how much time from the beginning of the reading did Efraim finish reading the five articles?

Given: 1 < x  (x and y are integers)
    1 < y
    \(\frac{x!}{y!} = x\)

x – y = ?

methods.text: Expand the top down to the bottom: \(x!=x\cdot(x-1)!\). The given says \(\frac{x!}{y!}=x\), so \(y!=(x-1)!\) and \(y=x-1\). The difference is 1.
Dividing one factorial by another leaves the run of integers between them. For the result to be a single factor \(x\), that run must be one term long — so the two factorials are neighbours.

questions.stem:
For every two numbers a and b that are different from zero, the operation $(a , b) was defined thus:
\($(a,b) = \frac{b^2}{a} + \frac{a^2}{b}\)

\(\dfrac{\$(-2\,,\ 3)}{\$(3\,,-2)} = ?\)

methods.text: \(\sqrt x = \frac12\) gives \(x = \frac14\), so \(x^2 = \frac{1}{16}\).
Square twice in total, not once: the given is already a square root, so reaching \(x^2\) means squaring the given and then squaring again.

questions.stem:
In right-angled and isosceles triangle ABC (AB = BC) a semicircle is inscribed of which DE is its diameter.
D and E are the midpoints of sides AB and BC respectively.
Given: The area of the semicircle (the dark area) is \(\pi\) cm².

What is the area of triangle ABC (in cm²)?
Elad multiplied the average of two numbers by the difference between them and obtained 8. What is the difference (in absolute value) between the squares of the numbers?

methods.text: The average times the difference is \(\dfrac{a+b}{2}(a-b) = \dfrac{a^2-b^2}{2}\). That equals 8, so the difference of the squares is 16.
Build a pair that fits: \(a=5, b=3\) has average 4 and difference 2, whose product is 8 as required. Then \(a^2-b^2 = 25-9 = 16\).
The question is the difference-of-squares identity stated in words. Recognising \(\frac{a+b}{2}\) and \(a-b\) as half the two factors is the whole problem.

Given: AB = BC , DE = EF

What is the volume of the dark prism (in cm³)?

On a certain stretch of road there are 20 cars. In 90% of the cars there is an air conditioner. In 60% of the cars exactly 3 people are sitting, and in the rest of the cars only one person is sitting. How many people, at the very least, are sitting in the cars in which there is an air conditioner?

methods.text:
18 cars have air conditioning and 12 cars hold 3 people, so 8 hold 1. To make the total as small as possible, put as many of the 1-person cars inside the air-conditioned set as you can — all 8.

That leaves 10 air-conditioned cars holding 3 each: \(30 + 8 = 38\).
“At the very least” means you choose the overlap, subject to the counts. The question is an optimisation, not a calculation.

questions.stem: In the accompanying figure is pentagon ABCDE and two of its diagonals. Inbar found all the quadrilaterals in the figure. How many quadrilaterals did Inbar find? (by "quadrilateral" what is meant is a simple quadrilateral, that is, whose sides do not intersect one another)
What is the smallest number of whole rectangles whose side lengths are 1 cm and 10 cm, that are needed in order to completely hide the isosceles trapezoid in the figure?
\(M = N^2 \cdot K\) Given: N is divisible by 3 without a remainder, and K is even. What is the greatest number by which M is divisible with certainty without a remainder?

methods.text: Track the prime factors. \(N\) divisible by 3 makes \(N^2\) divisible by \(3^2 = 9\); \(K\) even contributes a 2. So \(M = N^2 K\) is guaranteed \(9 \times 2 = 18\).
Not 36: that would need two factors of 2, and \(K\) is only guaranteed one. Take \(N=3,\ K=2\), giving \(M=18\) exactly — which also proves 18 is the most you can claim.

questions.stem: Given: | x + y | < | x – y | Which of the following expressions is necessarily negative?

methods.text: \(|x+y|<|x-y|\) says the sum cancels more than the difference does, and cancellation on adding happens exactly when the two numbers have opposite signs. Opposite signs means the product is negative.
Both sides are non-negative, so squaring is safe: \(x^2+2xy+y^2<x^2-2xy+y^2\) reduces to \(4xy<0\).

\(x=3,\ y=-1\) satisfies the given and makes \(y\), \(x+y\) and \(x-y\) come out negative, positive and positive. Swapping to \(x=-3,\ y=1\) flips all three but leaves \(xy\) negative — which is why only (2) survives.

questions.stem:
In the 7th grade there are 16 girls and 15 boys, in the 8th grade there are 17 girls and 16 boys, and in the 9th grade there are 18 girls and 17 boys.

In which grade is the relative proportion of the girls in the grade (out of all the boys and girls in the grade together) the greatest?
options: in all three grades there is the same relative proportion of girls

methods.text: Compare \(\frac{16}{31}\), \(\frac{17}{33}\), \(\frac{18}{35}\). Each is just over a half; the smallest denominator relative to its numerator wins.
Each grade has one more girl than boy, so each ratio is \(\frac{n}{2n-1}\) — and that decreases as \(n\) grows. The 7th grade, with the fewest pupils, has the highest proportion.
